notes.front: What is a conjugate prior? Give the Beta-Binomial update.
notes.back: A prior family closed under the likelihood's update. Beta(a, b) + k successes in n trials → Beta(a + k, b + n − k).
notes.analogy: The hyperparameters are pseudo-counts: the prior acts like a + b imaginary earlier trials.

notes.front: Beta-Binomial: why is the posterior mean a compromise?
notes.back: \(\frac{a+k}{a+b+n}\) is a weighted average of the prior mean \(\frac{a}{a+b}\) and the sample proportion \(\frac kn\), with weights a + b and n.

notes.front: Posterior predictive vs plug-in prediction?
notes.back: \(p(\tilde x\mid x)=\int p(\tilde x\mid\theta)\,p(\theta\mid x)\,d\theta\) averages over parameter uncertainty, so it is wider than plugging in \(\hat\theta\) (Normal: variance \(\sigma^2+\tau_n^2\)).
notes.extra:
Aleatoric noise plus epistemic (parameter) uncertainty; only the second shrinks with data.
Geometry: A plug-in forecast is one curve; the posterior predictive is a blurred bundle of curves. Law of total variance: aleatoric (within-model noise) plus epistemic (which model). Only the second shrinks with data.

notes.front: How does the marginal likelihood (evidence) implement an automatic Occam's razor?
notes.back: \(p(x\mid M)\) is the probability the model gave the data before seeing it. A flexible model spreads its mass over many possible datasets; a simple model that fits concentrates its mass and wins.
notes.extra:
Laplace view: evidence ≈ best-fit likelihood × (posterior volume / prior volume); the second factor is the Occam penalty.
Geometry: Laplace approximation: evidence ≈ best-fit likelihood × (posterior volume / prior volume). The second factor is the Occam penalty: how much of the prior's parameter space had to be thrown away to fit the data.

notes.front: What is a Bayes factor?
notes.back: \(BF_{10}=p(x\mid M_1)/p(x\mid M_0)\); posterior odds = Bayes factor × prior odds.
notes.extra: Geometry: A very wide prior under the alternative wastes almost all its mass on parameter values far from the data, so the alternative predicted the data poorly. Unlike posteriors, Bayes factors never forget the prior; improper priors make them undefined.

notes.front: What is the Jeffreys–Lindley paradox?
notes.back: With a point null and a diffuse prior under the alternative, a small p-value can coexist with a Bayes factor strongly favouring the null, increasingly so as n grows or the prior widens.
notes.extra: A very wide prior wastes its mass far from the data. Unlike posteriors, Bayes factors never forget the prior.

notes.front: What does the Bernstein–von Mises theorem say?
notes.back: Under regularity (fixed dimension, prior positive at the truth, correct model) the posterior → \(N(\hat\theta_{MLE},I(\theta_0)^{-1}/n)\): the prior washes out and credible sets become valid confidence sets.
notes.extra:
Fails when dimension grows with n, in nonparametric models, at boundaries, and under misspecification.
Geometry: The log-likelihood paraboloid sharpens at rate n while the log-prior stays fixed: eventually the prior looks flat on the scale of the likelihood peak. Fails when the dimension grows with n, in nonparametric models, at boundaries, and under misspecification (the posterior then has the wrong width: no sandwich correction).

notes.text: Bayes point estimates: the posterior mean minimises {{c1::squared error}}; the median minimises {{c2::absolute error}}; the mode (MAP) minimises {{c3::0–1 loss}} (in the limit).
notes.extra: Geometry: A density is "probability per unit volume", and what counts as a unit volume depends on the coordinate system. Mass is real; height is a coordinate artefact. In high dimensions the mode can sit in a region with negligible mass.

notes.front: What is the conceptual weakness of the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate?
notes.back: It is not invariant to reparameterisation (densities transform with a Jacobian, so the peak moves when you change coordinates), and it ignores posterior mass.
notes.extra: Mass is real; height is a coordinate artefact. In high dimensions the mode can sit where there is negligible mass.

notes.front: What is the Jeffreys prior, and its key property?
notes.back: \(p(\theta)\propto\sqrt{\det I(\theta)}\): invariant under reparameterisation, i.e. uniform on the statistical manifold measured with the Fisher metric. Bernoulli → Beta(½, ½).
notes.extra: Geometry: \(\sqrt{\det(\text{metric})}\) is the Riemannian volume element. The Jeffreys prior is the uniform distribution on the statistical manifold measured with the Fisher metric: equal prior mass to equal numbers of distinguishable distributions, regardless of how you label them.

notes.front: What does de Finetti's theorem say?
notes.back: An infinite exchangeable (order-invariant) sequence is a mixture of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) sequences: if order doesn't matter to you, you are acting as if there is an unknown parameter with a prior.
notes.extra: Geometry: If order does not matter to you, you are behaving as if there is an unknown parameter with a prior, and the data are i.i.d. given it. Parameters and priors are not metaphysical assumptions; they are a representation theorem for symmetric beliefs. Also the justification for hierarchical models (exchangeable groups).

notes.front: What is empirical Bayes?
notes.back: Estimate the prior's hyperparameters from the data by maximising the marginal likelihood, then compute posteriors as usual. Units borrow strength from each other; it understates uncertainty.
notes.extra:
James–Stein is empirical Bayes for the Normal-means problem.
Geometry: With many parallel problems (genes, schools, players), the ensemble of noisy estimates reveals the shape of the prior. Each unit then borrows strength from all the others. Understates uncertainty, since hyperparameter uncertainty is ignored.

notes.front: What is the Bayes-optimal decision?
notes.back: The action minimising posterior expected loss \(\int L(\theta,a)\,p(\theta\mid x)\,d\theta\). Inference and decision separate: one posterior serves any loss.
notes.extra:
With asymmetric loss (overstock cheap, stockout costly) the optimal action is a quantile, not the mean.
Geometry: The posterior is a map of where the truth might be; the loss says how much each kind of miss hurts. With asymmetric loss (overstocking cheap, stockout costly) the optimal action is a quantile, not the mean.

notes.front: Prior vs posterior predictive checks?
notes.back: Prior predictive: simulate data from the prior alone to catch priors implying absurd observables. Posterior predictive: simulate replicated data from the fit and compare a test statistic with the observed one to reveal misfit.
notes.extra: Geometry: Priors on parameters are hard to judge in parameter space; push them forward into data space, where you have intuition. A posterior predictive check asks whether the observed data would be a typical member of the cloud of datasets the fitted model generates. It uses the data twice, so it is conservative.

notes.front: Why does the typical set matter for Bayesian computation?
notes.back: In high dimensions almost all posterior mass lies in a thin shell away from the mode, so expectations come from that shell: maximum a posteriori (MAP) optimisation finds an atypical point, and samplers must explore the shell.
notes.extra: Geometry: For a d-dimensional standard Gaussian the shell sits at radius \(\sqrt d\). The mode is the top of a needle-thin peak: highest, but with essentially no ground around it. A divergent sampler transition signals a region of the shell with curvature too high to be explored.

notes.front: What is the Laplace approximation?
notes.back: A Gaussian at the maximum a posteriori (MAP) with covariance = inverse Hessian of the negative log-posterior: \(N(\hat\theta_{MAP},H^{-1})\). Purely local; poor for skewed, multimodal or boundary posteriors.
notes.extra: Geometry: Fit the osculating paraboloid to the log-posterior at its peak. Exact when the posterior is Gaussian, good when Bernstein-von Mises has kicked in, poor for skewed, multimodal or boundary posteriors. It is a purely local approximation; it knows nothing beyond the curvature at one point.

notes.front: How does Metropolis–Hastings work?
notes.back: Propose θ′ from q; accept with probability \(\min\!\big(1,\frac{p(\theta')q(\theta\mid\theta')}{p(\theta)q(\theta'\mid\theta)}\big)\), else stay. Only density ratios are needed, so the normaliser cancels.
notes.analogy: A hiker who always takes uphill steps and takes downhill steps with probability equal to the height ratio: time spent at each spot becomes proportional to its height.

notes.front: Why does Metropolis–Hastings target the right distribution?
notes.back: The acceptance rule enforces detailed balance \(p(\theta)T(\theta\to\theta')=p(\theta')T(\theta'\to\theta)\), which makes p the stationary distribution.

notes.front: What is Gibbs sampling, and when does it mix badly?
notes.back: Draw each coordinate (or block) from its full conditional in turn: Metropolis–Hastings with acceptance 1. Mixes badly when parameters are strongly correlated: axis-aligned steps crawl along a diagonal ridge.
notes.extra: Geometry: Moves are axis-aligned. In a narrow diagonal valley each axis-parallel step can only be as long as the valley is wide, so the sampler takes a tiny staircase along the ridge. Fixes: reparameterise/rotate, block correlated parameters, or use gradients.

notes.front: How does Hamiltonian Monte Carlo work, and why does it scale?
notes.back: Add a momentum variable, simulate Hamiltonian dynamics with the leapfrog integrator (using \(\nabla\log p\)), then Metropolis-accept. Energy is nearly conserved, so distant proposals are accepted.
notes.analogy: A frictionless puck flicked across the negative-log-posterior surface: it glides along the valley's contours instead of stumbling randomly.
notes.extra: Cost per independent draw ~d^(5/4) vs d² for random walk. No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) picks trajectory length automatically.

notes.front: What is Neal's funnel?
notes.back: In hierarchical models (\(\alpha_j\sim N(\mu,\tau)\)), small τ squeezes the α's together and large τ frees them: curvature varies by orders of magnitude, no single step size works, and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) reports divergences.
notes.extra: Geometry: The reparameterisation is a change of coordinates that straightens the funnel into something close to an isotropic blob: the prior dependence between τ and α is moved out of the geometry and into a deterministic transform. Use it when data per group is weak; centred is better when data is strong.

notes.front: How does the non-centred parameterisation fix the funnel, and when should you use it?
notes.back: Sample \(z_j\sim N(0,1)\) and set \(\alpha_j=\mu+\tau z_j\): the funnel straightens into a near-isotropic blob. Use it when data per group is weak.

notes.text: Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) diagnostics: {{c1::\(\hat R\)}} compares between- and within-chain variance (want < 1.01); {{c2::effective sample size (ESS)}} counts equivalent independent draws; {{c3::divergences}} (HMC) mean estimates are biased, not merely noisy.
notes.analogy: Search parties dropped at different spots: only when they all report the same territory do you trust the map.
notes.extra:
R-hat can only detect non-convergence, never prove convergence.
Geometry: \(\hat R\) is a one-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) across chains: if chains started in different places still disagree about where the mass is, none of them can be trusted. It can only detect non-convergence, never prove convergence.

notes.front: What does variational inference optimise?
notes.back: It picks q from a tractable family to minimise \(\mathrm{KL}(q\|p(\theta\mid x))\), by maximising the evidence lower bound (ELBO), since \(\log p(x)=\mathrm{ELBO}(q)+\mathrm{KL}(q\|p(\theta\mid x))\).
notes.extra:
Fast and scalable, but biased by the family's shape; mean-field typically underestimates variance.
Geometry: Inference turned into optimisation: project the true posterior onto the manifold of tractable distributions. Fast and scalable, but the answer is biased by the family's shape, typically underestimating variance (mean-field ignores correlations).

notes.front: Reverse Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence KL(q‖p) vs forward KL(p‖q) when fitting a unimodal q to a multimodal p?
notes.back: Reverse (variational inference): mode-seeking, locks onto one mode, too narrow. Forward (maximum likelihood, expectation propagation (EP)): mass-covering, straddles all modes and puts mass in the empty valley between them.
notes.extra: Geometry: the expectation is under the first argument. Under q you never look where q is zero, so ignoring a mode is free; under p you are inspected everywhere p lives.

notes.front: What is a Gaussian Process?
notes.back: A distribution over functions in which any finite set of function values is jointly Gaussian, specified by a mean function and a kernel \(k(x,x')\) that says how strongly nearby values are tied.
notes.extra: Geometry: An infinite-dimensional Gaussian ellipsoid over function space, sliced by the hyperplanes "function passes through these data points". The kernel says how strongly nearby function values are tied together; the predictive variance pinches to the noise level at data points and balloons back to the prior far from them.

notes.front: How does Gaussian process (GP) regression predict, and what does it cost?
notes.back: By Gaussian conditioning on the observed points: mean \(k_*^\top(K+\sigma^2I)^{-1}y\); the variance pinches near the data and returns to the prior far away. Cost \(O(n^3)\).

notes.front: How are Bayesian linear regression, ridge, kernel ridge and Gaussian process (GP) regression related?
notes.back: Bayesian linear regression with prior \(N(0,\tau^2I)\) has posterior mean = ridge (λ = σ²/τ²). Swapping x for features φ(x) induces a kernel; the GP posterior mean = kernel ridge, plus a predictive variance.
notes.extra: Geometry: Weight-space view: a Gaussian blob over coefficient vectors. Function-space view: the same blob pushed through the feature map becomes a Gaussian over functions. The kernel trick lets you work in function space even when the weight space is infinite-dimensional.

notes.front: How does importance sampling work?
notes.back: \(E_p[f]=E_q[f\,p/q]\): sample from q and reweight by \(w=p/q\). q needs heavier tails than p.
notes.analogy: Reweighting a biased survey: if young people were oversampled 2×, count each of their answers half.
notes.extra: Geometry: Two thin shells (the typical sets of p and q) in high-dimensional space barely overlap unless p and q are almost identical. Samples from q almost never land where p's mass is.

notes.front: Why does importance sampling break down in high dimensions?
notes.back: Weight variance grows exponentially with d: the typical sets of p and q barely overlap, so one sample carries nearly all the weight.

notes.front: Why is a training loss only a proxy, and what goes wrong because of it?
notes.back: You optimise what is differentiable (cross-entropy, squared error), not the business goal; the gap between proxy and goal is where models game the objective.
notes.extra: Example: Optimizing click-through rate as a proxy for 'user value' produces clickbait. Optimizing squared error on house prices lets a few mansions dominate the fit.

notes.front: What is the gradient-descent update, and what does the learning rate do?
notes.back: \(w\leftarrow w-\eta\nabla L(w)\): step against the gradient. Too small η crawls; too large overshoots the valley and oscillates or diverges.
notes.analogy: Walking downhill in fog: tiny steps take forever, giant leaps land you on the opposite slope.
notes.extra: Learning-rate schedules start big to move fast, then shrink to settle.

notes.front: Why use mini-batch (stochastic) gradients instead of the full-dataset gradient?
notes.back: A small random batch gives a noisy but unbiased estimate ~1,000× cheaper, so you take far more steps; the noise also helps escape sharp minima and saddle points.
notes.analogy: Polling 1,000 voters estimates the national mood at a fraction of the cost of asking everyone.

notes.front: With a constant learning rate η and batch size B, where does stochastic gradient descent (SGD) end up?
notes.back: Hovering in a noise ball of size ∝ η/B instead of converging; decaying η gives convergence. The noise biases it toward flat minima (implicit regularisation).
notes.analogy: A ball on a shaking landscape: it can't settle in narrow crevices but rests in wide basins. The "temperature" is η/B.
notes.extra: Linear scaling rule: keep η/B roughly constant when changing batch size.

notes.front: How does the condition number κ = L/μ control gradient-descent speed?
notes.back: In a long, narrow valley the gradient points mostly across it, so steps zigzag between the walls and crawl along the floor; the best fixed step converges at rate ≈ (κ−1)/(κ+1) per step.
notes.extra:
Step size is limited by the steepest direction, progress by the flattest.
Geometry: In a round bowl the gradient points at the minimum. In a long narrow valley it points mostly across the valley: the iterate zigzags between the walls and crawls along the floor. The step size is limited by the steepest direction, the progress by the flattest.

notes.front: How does Newton's method differ geometrically from gradient descent?
notes.back: \(\theta\leftarrow\theta-H^{-1}\nabla L\) rescales coordinates so the elliptical valley becomes round, then steps straight to the local quadratic's minimum. Quadratic convergence, but \(O(d^3)\) per step.
notes.extra:
Affine-invariant; can be attracted to saddles. Limited-memory Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno (L-BFGS), Gauss–Newton and natural gradient approximate it. Preconditioning = choosing a ruler under which the landscape is isotropic.
Geometry: Multiplying by \(H^{-1}\) is a change of coordinates that makes the elliptical valley round, after which the gradient points straight at the minimum. Preconditioning in general = choosing a ruler under which the landscape is isotropic.

notes.front: What does momentum add to stochastic gradient descent (SGD)?
notes.back: A running average of gradients: zigzag components across the valley cancel, components along the floor accumulate. Improves dependence on the condition number from κ to √κ.
notes.analogy: A heavy ball rolling down the valley rather than a hiker re-deciding every step.

notes.front: What does Adam add on top of momentum?
notes.back: Per-coordinate scaling by a running root mean square (RMS) of gradients: a cheap diagonal preconditioner, so step size is roughly scale-invariant per parameter. It can't fix valleys that run diagonally.

notes.front: Why are penalised and constrained forms of regularisation equivalent?
notes.back: Lagrangian duality: each λ ≥ 0 matches a budget t (\(\Omega(\beta)\le t\)) with the same solution. At the optimum the loss contour is tangent to the constraint boundary, and λ is the exchange rate.
notes.extra: Geometry: At the solution the loss contour is tangent to the constraint boundary: gradients are anti-parallel, \(\nabla L=-\lambda\nabla\Omega\). λ is the exchange rate between the two: how much loss you would save per unit relaxation of the budget.

notes.front: What is the natural gradient?
notes.back: \(F^{-1}\nabla L\), with F the Fisher information: steepest descent when step length is measured by Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between the model's distributions, not by parameter distance. Reparameterisation-invariant.
notes.extra:
Relatives: Fisher scoring, Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (K-FAC), trust region policy optimization (TRPO); Adam is a crude diagonal approximation.
Geometry: "Steepest" depends on what counts as a unit step. The Euclidean gradient assumes parameter space is flat with an arbitrary coordinate grid. The natural gradient uses the intrinsic ruler of the statistical manifold, under which equal-length steps change the model's predictions by equal amounts.

notes.front: What is overfitting, and how do you detect it?
notes.back: The model learns noise and quirks of the training data instead of the pattern: training error keeps falling while held-out error rises. Detect it with a validation set you never train on.
notes.analogy: A student who memorised last year's exam answers: 100% on that exam, fails a new one.

notes.front: What is underfitting, and its signature?
notes.back: The model is too simple or under-trained to capture the real pattern: both training and validation error are high.
notes.extra: Example: Fitting a straight line to seasonal traffic. The model cannot represent the weekly cycle no matter how much data you give it.

notes.front: Train / validation / test split: what is each for?
notes.back: Train: fit parameters. Validation: choose hyperparameters and model variants. Test: one final, untouched estimate of real-world performance.

notes.front: Why is tuning on the test set the cardinal sin?
notes.back: Every decision made by looking at it leaks information. After trying 50 configurations, the best test score is the max of 50 noisy draws: optimistic, expect it to drop in production.

notes.front: What is data leakage?
notes.back: Information unavailable at prediction time (from the future, the label, or the test set) sneaking into training features. Suspiciously good results usually mean leakage.
notes.extra: Example: A churn model with feature 'number of support tickets in the 30 days after signup' when churn is measured at day 30. Or an incident predictor trained with a 'severity' field that is only set after the incident. Suspiciously good results usually mean leakage.

notes.text: Common forms of data leakage: {{c1::random splits of time-series data}}; {{c2::preprocessing (scaling, imputation, feature selection) fitted on all data before splitting}}; {{c3::features that are consequences of the label}}; {{c4::duplicates or the same subject across splits}}.

notes.front: What does nested cross-validation prevent?
notes.back: Selection-induced optimism: the inner loop tunes hyperparameters, the outer loop evaluates the whole tuning procedure, so your choices never see the folds you report.
notes.extra:
Everything that looked at the data, including your own choices, is part of the "model" and must sit inside the CV loop.
Geometry: The minimum of several noisy estimates is biased low (winner's curse). Everything that looked at the data, including your own choices, is part of the "model" and must sit inside the cross-validation loop.

notes.front: State the bias–variance decomposition of expected squared error.
notes.back: Error = irreducible noise σ² + bias² (systematic miss of the model class) + variance (sensitivity to the particular training sample); expectation over training sets and noise.
notes.analogy: Archery: bias = arrows clustered tightly but off-centre; variance = arrows scattered around the bullseye.
notes.extra: Formula: \(E[(y-\hat f(x))^2]=\sigma^2+(E\hat f(x)-f(x))^2+\mathrm{Var}(\hat f(x))\).

notes.front: How do model complexity and training-set size shift bias and variance?
notes.back: More complexity: lower bias, higher variance. More data: lower variance, which makes complex models safe. The same architecture can overfit 1k rows and underfit 1B.

notes.text: Regularisation techniques: {{c1::L2 / weight decay}} shrinks weights; {{c2::L1}} sparsifies; {{c3::dropout}} randomly disables units; {{c4::data augmentation}} enlarges the effective dataset; {{c5::early stopping}} halts before memorisation.
notes.extra: All trade a little bias for less variance. Weight decay = maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation with a Gaussian prior.

notes.front: How does early stopping work, and why is it regularisation?
notes.back: Stop when validation loss starts rising even though training loss still falls. Fewer steps keep the weights near initialisation, limiting how much noise they can fit.

notes.front: What problem does k-fold cross-validation solve?
notes.back: A single validation split gives a noisy estimate on small data. Rotating k folds uses all data for both training and validation and shows the spread between folds.
notes.extra: Example: With 800 examples, a single 20% validation set is 160 examples—accuracy ±4% by chance alone. 5-fold CV averages over 5 such estimates and shows the variance between folds.

notes.front: Why must you always compare against a baseline?
notes.back: Absolute metrics mean nothing without what a trivial model achieves: majority class, the mean, "same as yesterday", a linear model, a hand-written rule.
notes.extra: Example: 'Our outage predictor is 99.5% accurate.' Outages happen 0.4% of the time, so 'always predict no outage' is 99.6% accurate. The model is worse than nothing.

notes.text: {{c1::Precision}} = of the items flagged, the fraction that were real. {{c2::Recall}} = of the real items, the fraction that were flagged.

notes.front: Raising a classifier's threshold trades what for what, and how do you choose?
notes.back: Higher threshold: more precision, less recall. Choose by the cost of each error: spam filters favour precision; intrusion detection and screening favour recall.
notes.analogy: A fishing net: precision is how much of your catch is actually fish; recall is how much of the lake's fish you caught. A finer net catches more fish and more junk.
notes.extra: F1 is the harmonic mean if you need one number.

notes.front: What does receiver operating characteristic (ROC) area under the curve (AUC) measure?
notes.back: The probability the model scores a random positive above a random negative: a pure ranking measure, invariant to class prevalence and monotone score transforms.
notes.extra: ROC plots true-positive rate vs false-positive rate over all thresholds. AUC equals the Mann–Whitney U statistic.

notes.front: Why prefer precision–recall curves over receiver operating characteristic (ROC) area under the curve (AUC) on heavily imbalanced data?
notes.back: ROC's false-positive rate is a fraction of a huge negative class, so a tiny rate hides many false alarms; precision exposes them.
notes.extra:
Example: AUC 0.95 for a fraud model at 0.1% fraud can still mean 50 false alarms per fraud caught.
Geometry: Two score histograms (positives, negatives); the threshold is a vertical line sweeping across. ROC traces the two tail areas against each other. AUC measures how little the histograms overlap, and is equivalent to the Mann-Whitney U statistic.

notes.front: What does it mean for a probabilistic model to be calibrated?
notes.back: Among predictions of 70%, about 70% turn out positive. It matters whenever the probability feeds a decision, threshold or expected-value calculation.
notes.analogy: A good weather forecaster: on the days they say 70% rain, it rains on about 70% of them.
notes.extra: Example: A model says 'this deploy has a 5% rollback risk'. If historically 30% of its '5%' deploys were rolled back, the number is useless for risk budgeting. Check with a reliability diagram; fix with temperature scaling or isotonic regression.

notes.front: Calibration vs discrimination?
notes.back: Discrimination: ranking positives above negatives (AUC). Calibration: probabilities match frequencies. They are independent: a monotone remap of scores changes calibration but not AUC.
notes.extra:
Post-hoc fixes: Platt scaling, isotonic regression, temperature scaling. Check with a reliability diagram.
Geometry: Reliability diagram: predicted probability versus observed frequency; calibration = hugging the diagonal. Any monotone remapping of scores leaves AUC unchanged but can repair calibration, so the two are orthogonal properties.

notes.front: What is a proper scoring rule?
notes.back: A score minimised in expectation by reporting the true probability: log loss, Brier score. Accuracy and area under the curve (AUC) are not proper.

notes.front: Why do production ML models silently rot?
notes.back: Distribution shift: production data drifts from training data (new users, new attacks, seasons, the model's own feedback loop), and the validation score stops applying, without any error.
notes.extra: Example: A fraud model trained pre-2020 sees a pandemic-era surge of first-time online shoppers and flags them all. Or a recommender changes what users see, which changes what they click, which changes the training data—feedback loop.

notes.text: Shift types: {{c1::covariate shift}}: p(x) changes, p(y|x) fixed (fix: importance weighting); {{c2::label shift}}: p(y) changes, p(x|y) fixed (fix: re-weight class priors); {{c3::concept drift}}: p(y|x) itself changes (fix: new labels, retraining, monitoring).
notes.extra: Geometry: Covariate shift moves the spotlight to a different part of the same function. Harmless for a correctly specified model, harmful for a misspecified one, because the best approximation (the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence projection) depends on where you look.

notes.text: Before trusting an ML result: is the {{c1::baseline}} fair and tuned? is the test set {{c2::truly held out}} (no leakage, no tuning on it)? is the gain bigger than {{c3::seed-to-seed or fold variance}}? how many {{c4::configurations were tried}}? does the test distribution {{c5::match deployment}}?
notes.extra: Example: "beats GPT-x by 3 points on benchmark Y": was Y in the training data? same prompting effort? is 3 points above seed variance?

notes.front: What is double descent?
notes.back: As model size grows, test error follows the classical U, spikes at the interpolation threshold (parameters ≈ samples), then falls again in the overparameterised regime, often below the classical minimum.

notes.front: Why does test error spike at the interpolation threshold and fall beyond it?
notes.back: At the threshold exactly one interpolator exists and its norm explodes to fit the noise. Beyond it, the optimiser picks the minimum-norm interpolator, which gets smoother as extra dimensions absorb the noise.
notes.extra: Geometry: At the threshold exactly one interpolating solution exists and it must contort to fit the noise; its norm explodes (the design matrix is nearly singular). Past the threshold there are infinitely many interpolators and the optimiser picks the minimum-norm one, which gets smoother as more dimensions become available to absorb the noise. Variance peaks at the threshold, then declines. Explicit regularisation flattens the spike.

notes.front: What is the practical reading of the No-Free-Lunch theorem?
notes.back: Averaged over all problems no learner wins. Every algorithm encodes an inductive bias, so choose models whose assumptions match the problem's structure.
notes.extra: Example: Convolutional networks assume nearby pixels matter together and patterns can appear anywhere; superb for images, wrong for tabular data where gradient-boosted trees, which assume axis-aligned splits, usually win.

notes.front: What is empirical risk minimisation, and the generalisation gap?
notes.back: ERM picks \(\hat f=\arg\min_{f\in\mathcal F}\hat R(f)\) (average training loss). Gap = true risk − empirical risk of \(\hat f\), controlled by the capacity of \(\mathcal F\) relative to n.
notes.extra:
The minimiser of a noisy landscape is biased low (winner's curse); uniform convergence bounds the worst dip over the class.
Geometry: \(\hat R\) is a noisy copy of the landscape R. Minimising over a big class means searching many places, and somewhere the noise will dip low by chance: the minimiser of a noisy function is biased downward (winner's curse). Uniform convergence bounds the worst dip over the class.

notes.text: Excess risk = {{c1::approximation error}} (model class too small) + {{c2::estimation error}} (sample too small) + {{c3::optimisation error}}.

notes.front: What is the Vapnik–Chervonenkis (VC) dimension, and its value for hyperplanes in \(\mathbb R^d\)?
notes.back: The size of the largest point set the class can shatter (realise all labelings). Hyperplanes: d + 1. The generalisation gap scales like \(O(\sqrt{\mathrm{VC}/n})\).
notes.extra:
A line can shatter 3 points but not the XOR labeling of a square's corners. Capacity ≠ parameter count: \(\sin(\omega x)\) has one parameter and infinite VC dimension.
Geometry: A line in the plane can shatter 3 points in general position but no set of 4: the XOR labeling of a square's corners cannot be split by a line. Capacity is measured by what labelings you can draw, not by counting parameters: \(\sin(\omega x)\) has one parameter and infinite VC dimension.

notes.front: What does a Support Vector Machine optimise?
notes.back: It maximises the margin: minimise \(\tfrac12\|w\|^2\) s.t. \(y_i(w^\top x_i+b)\ge1\) (margin width 2/‖w‖). Soft margin = hinge loss + L2 penalty.
notes.analogy: Find the widest street separating the two classes; the boundary is the centre line.

notes.front: What are support vectors?
notes.back: The points on or inside the margin. The solution depends only on them; removing any other point changes nothing.

notes.front: What is the kernel trick?
notes.back: Algorithms that use data only through inner products can replace \(x_i^\top x_j\) by \(k(x_i,x_j)=\langle\phi(x_i),\phi(x_j)\rangle\), working in a huge feature space without ever computing φ. Valid kernels are positive semidefinite.
notes.analogy: Points inside vs outside a circle can't be split by a line; lift them onto a paraboloid (add x₁² + x₂²) and a flat plane separates them.

notes.front: What does the representer theorem say?
notes.back: For losses regularised by a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) norm, the minimiser has the form \(f^*(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_ik(x_i,x)\): an infinite-dimensional search reduces to n coefficients.
notes.extra: Geometry: Decompose any candidate f into a part inside the span of the kernel functions at the data points and a part perpendicular to it. The perpendicular part does not change any fitted value \(f(x_i)\) (reproducing property) but adds to the norm. So it is pure cost: drop it. Same argument as minimum-norm interpolation.

notes.front: What does Principal Component Analysis (PCA) find?
notes.back: Orthogonal directions of maximum variance: the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, with eigenvalues = variance along each. The top k give the best k-dimensional linear approximation.
notes.analogy: Fit an ellipsoid to the data cloud; the principal components are its axes, longest first.
notes.extra: Example: 50 server metrics are collected, but most co-move with load. PCA might show 2 components explain 90% of the variance: 'overall load' and 'disk vs CPU bound'. Plot those 2 instead of 50 dashboards.

notes.front: Why are "maximise projected variance" and "minimise reconstruction error" the same PCA problem?
notes.back: Pythagoras: for centred data, total squared length = projected + residual, and the total is fixed.
notes.extra:
Computationally: the right singular vectors of centred \(X=UDV^\top\); variances are \(d_j^2/(n-1)\).
Geometry: Fit an ellipsoid to the data cloud; the principal components are its axes, longest first. Maximising projected variance and minimising perpendicular residual are the same problem by Pythagoras: total squared length = projected + residual, and the total is fixed.

notes.front: How does a linear autoencoder relate to PCA?
notes.back: With a k-dimensional bottleneck and squared loss it learns the same subspace as the top-k principal components (not necessarily the same basis).
notes.extra: Geometry: A nonlinear autoencoder fits a curved k-dimensional manifold instead of a flat subspace. The variational autoencoder (VAE)'s Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence term forces the codes to fill a standard Gaussian blob without holes, so that every point in latent space decodes to something sensible and you can sample.

notes.front: What does k-means minimise, and how does Lloyd's algorithm do it?
notes.back: Within-cluster sum of squared distances. Alternate: assign each point to its nearest centroid, then move each centroid to its points' mean. Converges to a local optimum (use k-means++ init).

notes.front: Why can't k-means find elongated or non-convex clusters?
notes.back: Its cluster regions are Voronoi cells: convex polytopes bounded by perpendicular bisectors between centroids. It is the hard-assignment, equal-spherical-variance limit of a Gaussian mixture.

notes.front: Gaussian mixture fitted by expectation–maximization (EM): what are the E- and M-steps?
notes.back: E: compute each point's responsibility per component (posterior membership). M: update weights, means and covariances as responsibility-weighted averages.
notes.extra:
Pitfalls: likelihood unbounded when a component collapses onto one point; label switching; local optima. A "soft Voronoi".
Geometry: Soft Voronoi: each point is shared among ellipsoids in proportion to how well each explains it. Each ellipsoid then re-fits itself to the points it partially owns. Boundaries between components are quadrics rather than flat faces.

notes.front: What function class does a decision tree represent?
notes.back: Piecewise-constant on axis-aligned boxes, with splits chosen greedily by impurity reduction (Gini or entropy; variance for regression). Low bias, very high variance.
notes.extra:
A diagonal boundary needs a staircase of cuts, so trees are inefficient for linear structure. Invariant to monotone feature transforms.
Geometry: Recursive guillotine cuts of a sheet of paper, each parallel to an axis. A diagonal boundary has to be approximated by a staircase, which is why trees are inefficient for linear structure and unstable to rotations of the features.

notes.front: Why does bagging reduce variance, and what limits it?
notes.back: Averaging B predictors with variance σ² and correlation ρ gives \(\rho\sigma^2+\frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2\): more trees kill only the second term; ρσ² is a floor.
notes.extra: Geometry: Vectors of equal length: if they all point the same way, their average is just as long; if they are mutually orthogonal, the average shrinks as \(1/\sqrt B\). Diversity among ensemble members is the resource being exploited.

notes.front: What does a random forest add to bagging?
notes.back: Restricting each split to a random subset of features decorrelates the trees (lowers ρ), at a small cost in bias.

notes.front: How does gradient boosting work?
notes.back: Additively fit shallow trees to pseudo-residuals (the negative loss gradient w.r.t. current predictions), adding each with shrinkage ν: gradient descent in function space.
notes.extra:
For squared loss the pseudo-residuals are ordinary residuals. Regularisers: shrinkage, subsampling, tree depth, early stopping.
Geometry: Gradient descent in function space. The "parameter vector" is the vector of predictions \((F(x_1),\dots,F(x_n))\); the negative gradient says how each prediction should move; the tree is the closest representable direction to that gradient (a projection onto the weak learner class). Bagging attacks variance; boosting attacks bias.

notes.front: Bagging vs boosting: which error does each mainly attack?
notes.back: Bagging averages independent high-variance models: attacks variance. Boosting sequentially fits the residuals of weak models: attacks bias.

notes.front: In k-nearest neighbours, what controls the bias–variance trade-off?
notes.back: k: k = 1 has zero training error and high variance; large k is smooth with high bias. Feature scaling is part of the model, since everything depends on the distance metric.
notes.extra:
1-NN decision regions are the Voronoi tessellation of the training set. In high dimensions the "nearest" neighbour is almost as far as the farthest.
Geometry: The 1-NN decision regions are the Voronoi tessellation of the training set. Increasing k blurs the tessellation. All distance-based methods are hostage to the choice of metric, so scaling features is part of the model.

notes.front: When does a Gaussian generative classifier give a linear boundary?
notes.back: When the classes share a covariance Σ (LDA): the log-odds are linear, with \(w=\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_0)\). Different covariances give a quadratic boundary (QDA).
notes.extra: Geometry: Whiten the space with \(\Sigma^{-1/2}\) so both classes become spheres; then classify to the nearest centroid. The boundary is the perpendicular bisector in whitened space, which looks tilted back in the original space.

notes.front: linear discriminant analysis (LDA) vs logistic regression?
notes.back: Same linear form. LDA fits the joint density (more efficient if the Gaussian assumption holds); logistic regression fits the conditional likelihood (more robust when it doesn't).

notes.front: Why is cross-entropy the standard classification loss?
notes.back: It is the negative log-likelihood of a categorical model (so maximum likelihood = Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence minimisation), and with softmax its gradient w.r.t. the logits is simply \(p-y\).
notes.extra:
Example: true label "cat": predicting 0.9 costs −log₂ 0.9 ≈ 0.15 bits; predicting 0.1 costs −log₂ 0.1 ≈ 3.3 bits. Confident wrong answers are punished hardest.
Geometry: Softmax maps logit space onto the probability simplex; adding a constant to all logits changes nothing (one redundant direction). Temperature scales distance from the simplex centre: low T pushes toward a vertex, high T pulls toward the centroid.

notes.front: What is the manifold hypothesis?
notes.back: Real high-dimensional data (images, text, audio) lies near a low-dimensional manifold, so the intrinsic dimension, not the ambient one, governs how much data learning needs.
notes.analogy: A crumpled sheet of paper in 3-D is still 2-D to an ant walking on it.

notes.front: What can't you read from a t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding (t-SNE) or uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) plot?
notes.back: Cluster sizes, distances between clusters and apparent density: these methods preserve only local neighbourhoods, and results depend on perplexity/neighbour count and seed.

notes.front: What function does a rectified linear unit (ReLU) network compute, geometrically?
notes.back: A continuous piecewise-linear function: each neuron's hyperplane splits input space, together tiling it into convex polytopes with one affine map on each.
notes.analogy: Origami: each layer folds space along hyperplanes, and later cuts are replicated across all earlier folds, so linear regions can grow exponentially with depth.

notes.front: What does the universal approximation theorem say, and not say?
notes.back: One wide enough hidden layer can approximate any continuous function on a compact set. It says nothing about how many units, whether training finds the weights, or whether the fit generalises.
notes.extra: Geometry: Sums of shifted ramps or bumps can build any shape, like a Riemann sum or a Fourier series. Existence of a representation is cheap; the questions that matter are efficiency (depth) and learnability.

notes.front: What is backpropagation?
notes.back: Reverse-mode automatic differentiation: the forward pass stores activations; the backward pass propagates ∂L/∂node via vector-Jacobian products. The full gradient costs ≈ 2–3× a forward pass, whatever the parameter count.
notes.extra: Memory scales with depth (stored activations).

notes.front: Why reverse mode rather than forward mode for training networks?
notes.back: One scalar loss, millions of inputs: multiplying Jacobians from the output side keeps the running quantity a vector. Forward mode suits one input and many outputs.

notes.front: Why do gradients vanish or explode in deep networks?
notes.back: The backpropagated gradient is a product of layer Jacobians: singular values typically < 1 shrink it exponentially with depth; > 1 blow it up.
notes.extra:
Stable training needs Jacobians close to isometries (singular values near 1).
Geometry: Repeatedly applying a linear map stretches along some directions and squashes along others; after many applications only the extreme directions survive. Stable training needs layer Jacobians that are close to isometries (singular values near 1: "dynamical isometry").

notes.text: Remedies for vanishing/exploding gradients: {{c1::variance-preserving initialisation}}, {{c2::non-saturating (ReLU-family) activations}}, {{c3::residual connections}}, {{c4::normalisation layers}}, {{c5::gradient clipping}}, and gating (long short-term memory (LSTM)/gated recurrent unit (GRU)).

notes.front: What is the principle behind Xavier/Glorot and He initialisation?
notes.back: Choose weight variance so activation (forward) and gradient (backward) variances are preserved across layers: Xavier \(2/(n_{in}+n_{out})\); He \(2/n_{in}\) for rectified linear unit (ReLU) (× 2 because ReLU zeroes half the inputs).
notes.extra: Geometry: A sum of \(n\) independent terms has variance \(n\) times that of each term, so weights need variance ∝ 1/n for the pre-activation to stay order one. Makes each random layer approximately length-preserving at the start of training.

notes.front: BatchNorm vs LayerNorm?
notes.back: Both standardise activations, then apply a learned scale and shift. BatchNorm: statistics across the batch, per feature (train ≠ inference, weak with small batches). LayerNorm: across features, per example; standard in Transformers (often RMSNorm).
notes.extra:
Effect: a smoother, better-conditioned loss landscape and larger usable learning rates.
Geometry: LayerNorm projects each activation vector onto the hyperplane perpendicular to \((1,\dots,1)\) and then onto a sphere of radius \(\sqrt d\): only the direction survives. It also makes the loss invariant to the scale of the preceding weights, so weight norm only affects the effective learning rate.

notes.front: How does dropout regularise?
notes.back: Training zeroes each unit with probability p (survivors scaled by 1/(1−p)), approximating an ensemble of weight-sharing subnetworks and preventing co-adaptation; all units are used at test time.
notes.analogy: A team where random members call in sick each day learns not to depend on any single person.
notes.extra:
Keeping dropout on at test time gives Monte Carlo uncertainty estimates.
Geometry: Each training step projects the hidden representation onto a random coordinate subspace. A solution that survives all such projections cannot depend on any single coordinate: information must be spread redundantly.

notes.front: Why does decoupled weight decay (AdamW) differ from L2 regularisation in Adam?
notes.back: In Adam an L2 gradient term is divided by \(\sqrt{\hat v}\), so parameters with large gradients get regularised less. AdamW applies \(\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\lambda\theta\) outside the adaptive rescaling: uniform decay.
notes.extra:
For plain stochastic gradient descent (SGD) the two coincide.
Geometry: L2-in-the-loss pulls toward the origin in Adam's warped per-coordinate metric; decoupled decay pulls toward the origin in plain Euclidean space.

notes.front: Why do residual connections make very deep networks trainable?
notes.back: \(x_{l+1}=x_l+f(x_l)\) has Jacobian \(I+\partial f/\partial x\), so gradients flow through the identity path at any depth, and each block only learns a correction.
notes.analogy: Editing a draft instead of rewriting it from scratch at every layer: each block only adds a correction.
notes.extra:
Like Euler steps of an ODE. In Transformers the residual stream is a shared bus that layers read from and write to.
Geometry: An Euler discretisation of an ordinary differential equation \(\dot x=f(x,t)\): the representation flows through space in small steps rather than being replaced wholesale at each layer. Also behaves like an ensemble of paths of many different lengths. In Transformers the residual stream is a shared communication bus that layers read from and write to.

notes.text: Inductive biases of a convolutional layer: {{c1::locality}} (each output sees a small neighbourhood) and {{c2::weight sharing}} (the same filter everywhere), which give {{c3::translation equivariance}}; pooling adds approximate translation invariance.
notes.extra:
A fully connected layer constrained to commute with translations is forced to be a convolution; generalises to other groups (graphs, rotations).
Geometry: Sliding one template across the image and recording the match (inner product) at each location. It is a fully connected layer constrained by symmetry: requiring that the linear map commutes with translations forces it to be a convolution. Generalises to other groups (rotations, permutations giving graph networks).

notes.front: How do learned embeddings represent meaning?
notes.back: Concepts correspond to directions; similarity is cosine; relations can appear as roughly constant offsets (king − man + woman ≈ queen).
notes.extra: Geometry: Random unit vectors in d dimensions have cosine of order \(1/\sqrt d\): almost everything is almost perpendicular to almost everything else. The price is that individual neurons respond to many unrelated features (polysemanticity).

notes.front: How can a d-dimensional space hold far more than d features (superposition)?
notes.back: High dimensions allow exponentially many nearly orthogonal directions (Johnson–Lindenstrauss); if features are sparse, their interference is tolerable. Cost: polysemantic neurons.

notes.front: What does the loss landscape of a large neural network look like?
notes.back: High-loss critical points are overwhelmingly saddles, not local minima; minima have similar low loss and connect through low-loss valleys; flat minima tend to generalise better.
notes.extra: Geometry: For a critical point to be a minimum, all d Hessian eigenvalues must be positive. If signs were coin flips, that probability is \(2^{-d}\). In a million dimensions there is almost always some direction that leads downhill. Flat minimum: a wide basin, where a small shift between the training and test landscapes changes the loss little.

notes.front: What is the implicit bias of gradient descent?
notes.back: Among many zero-training-loss solutions it selects particular ones: the minimum-L2-norm interpolator for linear regression from zero init; the max-margin direction for logistic regression on separable data.
notes.extra:
The regulariser is the algorithm and its starting point, not a term in the loss.
Geometry: The set of interpolating solutions is a huge manifold; gradient descent from a small initialisation lands near the point of that manifold closest to where it started. The regulariser is the algorithm and its starting point, not a term in the loss.

notes.front: What is the Neural Tangent Kernel ("lazy training") regime?
notes.back: Infinitely wide networks trained with small learning rates behave like kernel regression with a fixed kernel. Real networks also learn features, which the NTK can't explain.

notes.front: What does a Variational Autoencoder add to an autoencoder?
notes.back: A probabilistic encoder/decoder trained on the evidence lower bound (ELBO) (reconstruction − Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence to a Gaussian prior) with the reparameterisation trick \(z=\mu+\sigma\odot\epsilon\); the KL term fills latent space so you can sample from it.

notes.front: What game does a generative adversarial network (GAN) play?
notes.back: A generator and a discriminator play a minimax game; with an optimal discriminator the generator minimises the Jensen–Shannon divergence to the data distribution.

notes.front: generative adversarial network (GAN) failure modes, and the Wasserstein fix?
notes.back: Mode collapse, oscillation, and vanishing generator gradients when D wins. Non-overlapping manifolds make Jensen–Shannon (JS) divergence flat; Wasserstein (earth-mover) distance still slopes toward the data.

notes.front: How do diffusion models generate data?
notes.back: Train a network to predict the Gaussian noise added to data at many noise levels; generate by starting from pure noise and denoising step by step.

notes.front: What does a diffusion model's noise prediction actually estimate?
notes.back: The score \(\nabla_x\log p_t(x)\) (Tweedie / denoising score matching): a vector field pointing toward the data manifold, defined everywhere thanks to multi-scale noise.

notes.front: What does contrastive learning (InfoNCE) optimise?
notes.back: A softmax classification of which candidate is the anchor's true positive. On the unit hypersphere it pulls positive pairs together (alignment) and spreads everything else out (uniformity). Used in SimCLR, CLIP.
notes.extra: Geometry: Embeddings are normalised to the unit hypersphere. The loss decomposes into alignment (pull positive pairs together) and uniformity (spread everything else evenly over the sphere). Temperature τ sets how strongly hard negatives are emphasised.

notes.front: Define a Markov Decision Process and the Markov property.
notes.back: A tuple \((\mathcal S,\mathcal A,P,R,\gamma)\): states, actions, transition kernel, reward, discount. Markov property: the future is conditionally independent of the past given the current state.
notes.extra:
The state is a sufficient statistic of history. If observations aren't Markov (one video frame has no velocity), enlarge the state.
Geometry: The state is a sufficient statistic of history for predicting the future. If what you observe is not Markov (one video frame has no velocity), enlarge the state (stack frames, use a recurrent memory, or a belief state).

notes.front: What is the discounted return, and what horizon does γ imply?
notes.back: \(G_t=\sum_{k\ge0}\gamma^kR_{t+k+1}\); effective horizon ≈ \(1/(1-\gamma)\) steps (γ = 0.99 → ~100, γ = 0.9 → ~10).
notes.extra: Geometry: An exponentially decaying window over the future. \(\gamma=0.99\) sees about 100 steps ahead, \(\gamma=0.9\) about 10.

notes.front: Besides setting a horizon, what roles does the discount γ play?
notes.back: Makes infinite-horizon sums finite, equals a per-step termination probability 1 − γ, and trades lower variance of return estimates for myopia.

notes.front: Define V, Q and the advantage A in reinforcement learning (RL).
notes.back: \(V^\pi(s)\): expected return from s under π. \(Q^\pi(s,a)\): expected return taking a first, then π. \(A=Q-V\): how much better a is than π's average action (\(E_\pi[A]=0\)).
notes.analogy: V is a state's altitude on the landscape of future reward; Q is the altitude you reach with a specific first step; A strips out "this state is just good".

notes.front: Bellman expectation equation in matrix form, and its solution?
notes.back: \(V^\pi=R^\pi+\gamma P^\pi V^\pi\), so \(V^\pi=(I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}R^\pi\); invertible because \(\gamma P^\pi\) has spectral radius ≤ γ < 1.
notes.extra:
A state's value = immediate reward + discounted average value of where it leads; values diffuse backward from the rewards.
Geometry: A self-consistency condition: a state's value = immediate reward + discounted average value of the neighbours it leads to. The Neumann series reads: reward now, plus reward one step out, plus two steps out. Values diffuse backward along the transition graph from where the rewards are.

notes.front: Why does value iteration converge?
notes.back: The Bellman optimality operator is a γ-contraction in the sup norm, so by Banach's fixed-point theorem it has a unique fixed point V*, and the error shrinks by γ each iteration.
notes.analogy: Repeatedly photocopying at 90%: every starting image collapses onto the same dot.

notes.front: How does policy iteration work, and why does it terminate?
notes.back: Alternate evaluating \(V^\pi\) and acting greedily w.r.t. \(Q^\pi\). Greedy improvement never lowers value anywhere (policy improvement theorem), so it reaches π* in finitely many, usually few, steps.
notes.extra: Geometry: The set of achievable value functions forms a polytope whose vertices are deterministic policies. Policy iteration hops from vertex to a better vertex, reaching the top corner \(V^*\) that dominates all others. It behaves like Newton's method on the Bellman equation, whereas value iteration is a fixed-point iteration.

notes.front: What is generalised policy iteration?
notes.back: Any interleaving of partial evaluation and partial improvement; nearly every reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm (e.g. actor-critic) is an instance.

notes.front: Monte Carlo vs temporal difference (TD) learning TD(0) value estimation?
notes.back: MC targets the full observed return: unbiased, high variance, needs complete episodes. TD(0) targets \(r+\gamma V(s')\): bootstraps from its own estimate, biased, low variance, online.
notes.analogy: MC waits until you arrive to judge the commute; TD revises the arrival estimate the moment you hit a traffic jam.

notes.front: What is the temporal difference (TD) error?
notes.back: \(\delta_t=r_{t+1}+\gamma V(s_{t+1})-V(s_t)\): a reward-prediction surprise (better or worse than expected). Update \(V(s_t)\leftarrow V(s_t)+\alpha\delta_t\).
notes.extra:
Dopamine neurons appear to encode this signal.
Geometry: δ is a surprise signal: things went better or worse than expected. It is the reward prediction error that dopamine neurons appear to encode. λ is a slider for how far back in time a surprise assigns credit.

notes.front: How do n-step returns and temporal difference (TD) learning TD(λ) interpolate between TD and Monte Carlo?
notes.back: n-step: n real rewards, then bootstrap. The λ-return geometrically averages all n-step returns: λ = 0 is TD(0), λ = 1 is Monte Carlo. Eligibility traces implement it online.

notes.front: Q-learning vs state–action–reward–state–action (SARSA)?
notes.back: Q-learning (off-policy) targets \(\max_{a'}Q(s',a')\), learning Q* regardless of behaviour. SARSA (on-policy) targets the action actually taken, so it values the policy including its exploration.
notes.analogy: Cliff walking: Q-learning learns the edge path and keeps falling off while exploring; SARSA prices in its own missteps and walks inland. Q-learning evaluates the ideal you, SARSA the actual you.

notes.front: Bandits: how does ε-greedy explore, and what regret does it get?
notes.back: Take a random action with probability ε: undirected exploration, linear regret for a fixed ε.
notes.extra: Geometry: Each arm has an estimate with an error bar. Upper confidence bound (UCB) ranks arms by the top of the bar: an arm is tried either because it looks good or because its bar is wide, and trying it shrinks the bar. Thompson sampling picks each arm with exactly the probability that it is the best one.

notes.front: Bandits: how does upper confidence bound (UCB) choose an arm?
notes.back: Highest estimate plus uncertainty bonus, \(\hat\mu_a+\sqrt{2\ln t/n_a}\) ("optimism in the face of uncertainty"): an arm is tried because it looks good or because its error bar is wide. Logarithmic regret.

notes.front: Bandits: how does Thompson sampling choose an arm?
notes.back: Sample a model from the posterior and act greedily for it, so each arm is played with the probability that it is best. Logarithmic regret; usually the best in practice (e.g. adaptive A/B tests).
notes.extra: Lai–Robbins: O(log T) regret is the optimal rate.

notes.text: reinforcement learning (RL)'s "deadly triad": {{c1::function approximation}} + {{c2::bootstrapping}} (temporal difference (TD) targets) + {{c3::off-policy training}}. Any two are safe; all three can diverge.
notes.extra: Geometry: the Bellman backup leaves the space of representable value functions and is projected back. On-policy that composition contracts; off-policy the weighting mismatches and it can expand.

notes.front: Which two tricks stabilise Deep Q-Networks, and why?
notes.back: Experience replay: random minibatches from a buffer break temporal correlation and reuse data. Target network: a slowly updated copy computes bootstrap targets so they don't move every step.
notes.analogy: Without a target network you regress onto a label that shifts with every update: a dog chasing its own tail.

notes.front: What is maximisation bias in Q-learning, and how does Double Q-learning fix it?
notes.back: Using the same noisy estimates to select and to evaluate the best action overestimates (E[max] ≥ max E). Double Q selects with one estimator and evaluates with another.
notes.analogy: Winner's curse: the highest of several noisy measurements is probably an overestimate; re-measure the winner with an independent instrument.

notes.front: What does the policy gradient theorem say, and why is it remarkable?
notes.back: \(\nabla J=E[\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a\mid s)\,Q^\pi(s,a)]\): no derivative of the dynamics or state distribution is needed, so it can be estimated from samples of a black-box environment.
notes.analogy: "Do more of what worked, less of what didn't": push up the log-probability of each action in proportion to how well it turned out.
notes.extra: REINFORCE uses the sampled return in place of Q.

notes.front: Why does subtracting a baseline in policy gradients keep the estimate unbiased but cut variance?
notes.back: \(E_\pi[\nabla\log\pi(a\mid s)\,b(s)]=b(s)\nabla\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)=0\), so b(s) adds no bias. With b = V the weight becomes the advantage, removing "this state is just good" noise.
notes.extra: Geometry: The expected score is zero, so the baseline is a control variate: a zero-mean term correlated with the noise. If every reward is around +100, raw REINFORCE pushes up every sampled action and relies on tiny differences; centring asks the right question: better or worse than average?

notes.front: What is an actor-critic method?
notes.back: The actor is a policy updated by policy gradient; the critic is a learned value function supplying low-variance advantage estimates in place of Monte Carlo returns.
notes.extra: Geometry: Generalised policy iteration with function approximators: the critic is approximate policy evaluation, the actor approximate policy improvement. λ dials how much you trust the critic versus the actual observed rewards.

notes.front: What does Generalised Advantage Estimation's λ trade off?
notes.back: \(\hat A_t=\sum_l(\gamma\lambda)^l\delta_{t+l}\): λ = 0 is one-step temporal difference (TD) (low variance, biased by critic error); λ = 1 is Monte Carlo (unbiased, high variance).

notes.front: What problem do trust-region policy methods (trust region policy optimization (TRPO), proximal policy optimization (PPO)) solve?
notes.back: A too-large policy step can collapse performance, and data from the old policy can't reveal it; equal parameter steps can mean very unequal behaviour changes. So limit the step in distribution (KL) space.
notes.extra: Geometry: Measure step size in distribution space (a KL ball around the current policy), not in parameter space. The surrogate objective is only a trustworthy local map near the old policy; the trust region is the area where the map is still accurate.

notes.front: trust region policy optimization (TRPO) vs proximal policy optimization (PPO): how does each limit the step?
notes.back: TRPO maximises the importance-ratio surrogate subject to \(\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{\text{old}}\|\pi_\theta)\le\delta\) (a natural-gradient step). PPO clips the ratio to [1 − ε, 1 + ε] so there is no incentive to move far.

notes.front: On-policy vs off-policy learning?
notes.back: On-policy learns about the policy generating the data (state–action–reward–state–action (SARSA), proximal policy optimization (PPO)): stable, sample-hungry. Off-policy learns a target policy from another behaviour policy's data (Q-learning, deep Q-network (DQN), soft actor-critic (SAC)): enables replay buffers and learning from logs.
notes.extra: Geometry: A product of many ratios is a random walk in log space; after T steps a few trajectories carry all the weight. One-step Q-learning avoids the ratios because its target conditions on the action and takes the max itself.

notes.front: Why are importance-sampling corrections hard in off-policy reinforcement learning (RL)?
notes.back: The product of per-step ratios π/μ has variance growing exponentially with the horizon; remedies truncate the ratios (Retrace, V-trace).

notes.front: Promise and central difficulty of model-based reinforcement learning (RL)?
notes.back: Learn the dynamics and plan (Dyna, model predictive control (MPC), Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) as in AlphaZero/MuZero) for far better sample efficiency. But one-step errors compound over rollouts, and the planner actively exploits model errors.
notes.analogy: Planning on a map is free, but an optimiser hunting for shortcuts finds exactly the places where the cartographer made mistakes.
notes.extra: Mitigations: short rollouts, model ensembles with uncertainty penalties, replanning every step.

notes.front: How is a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) reduced to a Markov decision process (MDP)?
notes.back: Use the belief state b(s) = P(s | history), updated by Bayes filtering: it is a sufficient statistic, and the belief process is a continuous-state MDP.
notes.extra:
The optimal value over beliefs is piecewise linear and convex: certainty is valuable, which is why information-gathering actions can be optimal.
Geometry: The belief is a point in the probability simplex over states. Value = upper envelope of hyperplanes (one per conditional plan). Convexity means certainty is valuable: corners of the simplex are worth more than the centre, which is why information-gathering actions can be optimal despite yielding no reward.

notes.front: Which reward shaping is guaranteed to preserve the optimal policy?
notes.back: Potential-based shaping \(F=\gamma\Phi(s')-\Phi(s)\): it telescopes along any trajectory, so it reshapes the hills without moving the summit.
notes.extra:
Any non-conservative bonus creates cycles the agent can farm forever.
Geometry: Shaping terms telescope along any trajectory: the total added reward depends only on the endpoints, like a conservative force field. It reshapes the hills to make them easier to climb without moving the summit. Any non-conservative bonus creates cycles the agent can farm forever.

notes.front: What is reward hacking?
notes.back: The agent maximises the literal reward in unintended ways (specification gaming; Goodhart's law).

notes.front: What is maximum-entropy RL (Soft Actor-Critic)?
notes.back: Maximise reward + α × policy entropy. The optimal policy is Boltzmann, \(\pi\propto\exp(Q_{\text{soft}}/\alpha)\), and the Bellman max becomes a log-sum-exp. Gives principled exploration and robustness.
notes.extra: Geometry: "Control as inference": condition a graphical model on optimality and the posterior over trajectories is this policy; it is Kullback-Leibler (KL)-regularised reinforcement learning toward a uniform prior. The temperature α melts the argmax vertex of the simplex into a smooth interior point; α → 0 recovers standard reinforcement learning.

notes.front: What is the core difficulty of offline RL?
notes.back: The backup's \(\max_{a'}Q(s',a')\) queries actions never seen in the data; their values are unconstrained extrapolations, the max picks the most overestimated, and no new data ever corrects it.
notes.extra: Geometry: The data covers only a thin tube of state-action space. Outside the tube the Q-function is unconstrained fantasy, and an optimiser is drawn to fantasy. Offline reinforcement learning is constrained optimisation: improve as much as possible while staying inside the tube.

notes.front: Remedies in offline reinforcement learning (RL)?
notes.back: Stay near the behaviour policy (behaviour-cloning regularisation), be pessimistic (conservative Q-learning (CQL) pushes Q down on unseen actions), or penalise uncertainty.
notes.analogy: The data covers a thin tube of state-action space; improve as much as possible while staying inside the tube.

notes.front: What is the occupancy-measure (linear programming) view of a Markov decision process (MDP)?
notes.back: Return is linear in the discounted state-action occupancy ρ, and valid occupancies form a polytope (flow-conservation constraints): solving the MDP is a linear programme whose dual variables are V(s).

notes.front: Why does an optimal deterministic policy always exist (linear programming (LP) view)?
notes.back: A linear objective over a polytope is maximised at a vertex, and the vertices correspond to deterministic policies.

notes.front: What is the credit assignment problem?
notes.back: Working out which earlier actions caused a delayed outcome; with sparse, delayed reward the learning signal per decision is tiny and noisy.

notes.front: How do value functions address credit assignment?
notes.back: They act as a potential field that turns a distant reward into immediate temporal difference (TD) errors (local slopes). Also: eligibility traces, advantages, discounting, shaping, hindsight relabelling, hierarchy.
